content: 1. Patients under the age of 30 without cirrhosis and with persistently normal or abnormal ALT levels, regardless of HBeAg status, may not require immediate antiviral treatment. However, their condition should be monitored closely to assess disease progression. 2. Decompensated cirrhosis is characterized by clinical features such as portal hypertension (ascites, variceal hemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency (jaundice). Other signs of advanced liver disease or cirrhosis may include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pruritus, fatigue, arthralgia, palmar erythema, and edema. 3. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined by the persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for six months or more. The age threshold of 30 years for treatment consideration is not absolute, as some individuals under 30 may also meet criteria for antiviral therapy. 4. ALT levels in CHB patients can fluctuate, necessitating longitudinal monitoring to identify trends. The upper limit of normal ALT is defined as below 30 U/L for men and 19 U/L for women, based on sensitivity for detecting liver histological disease in hepatitis B. Local laboratory reference ranges should also be considered. 5. Persistently normal or abnormal ALT levels are defined as three ALT measurements below or above the upper limit of normal, taken at unspecified intervals over a 6–12-month period or at predefined intervals during a 12-month period. 6. In settings where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, other common causes of persistently elevated ALT levels, such as impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidemia, and fatty liver, should be excluded. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established an international standard for expressing HBV DNA concentrations in IU/mL to ensure comparability. The same assay should be used consistently in the same patient to evaluate antiviral efficacy. 8. HBV DNA values reported in copies/mL can be converted to IU/mL by dividing by a factor of 5 (e.g., 10,000 copies/mL = 2,000 IU/mL; 100,000 copies/mL = 20,000 IU/mL; 1 million copies/mL = 200,000 IU/mL). 9. Extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis B, such as glomerulonephritis or vasculitis, may also warrant treatment initiation. 10. The decision to initiate antiviral therapy is typically based on a combined assessment of liver disease stage (from clinical features or non-invasive tests), serum ALT levels, and HBV DNA levels. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) quantification of serum HBV DNA measures viral replication and correlates with disease progression. 11. Antiviral therapy aims to prevent adverse outcomes of CHB. Treatment decisions are straightforward in patients with life-threatening or advanced liver disease, such as acute liver failure, compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, or acute-on-chronic liver failure. 12. In patients without cirrhosis, antiviral therapy should target those at the highest risk of disease progression (fibrosis), while those with minimal fibrosis and low risk of CHB progression should be identified as not requiring treatment. 13. During the immune-tolerant phase of CHB, HBV DNA levels are high, but ALT levels are low or normal, with minimal liver inflammation or fibrosis progression. In the immune-active phase, HBV DNA levels decrease, but ALT levels rise, increasing the risk of fibrosis progression. 14. The 2015 WHO HBV guidelines recommend prioritizing antiviral therapy for individuals with life-threatening liver disease (decompensated cirrhosis) and compensated cirrhosis, regardless of ALT or HBV DNA levels. 15. For individuals without cirrhosis, treatment should be targeted at those with persistently abnormal ALT levels and HBV DNA levels >20,000 IU/mL, especially in those over 30 years of age, regardless of HBeAg status. 16. Treatment is not recommended for individuals with minimal liver disease or fibrosis, low risk of progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), persistently normal ALT levels, and low HBV replication (<2,000 IU/mL). 17. In settings with limited access to HBV DNA testing, treatment decisions rely on clinical features and serum ALT levels. Persistently abnormal ALT levels should prompt treatment initiation after excluding other causes of elevated ALT. 18. Monitoring during and after treatment is essential to assess adherence, evaluate sustained viral suppression, and detect disease progression or reactivation. Retreatment is recommended if there are consistent signs of reactivation, such as increased ALT levels, detectable HBV DNA, or seroreversion to HBsAg or HBeAg positivity. 19. Regular monitoring of ALT, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels (where available) is recommended at least annually. Non-invasive tests, such as APRI or transient elastography, should be used to assess for cirrhosis progression. 20. More frequent monitoring is advised for individuals with advanced disease (compensated or decompensated cirrhosis), during the first year of treatment, or after treatment discontinuation to detect severe exacerbations. 21. The cost of regular ALT and HBV DNA monitoring is a significant consideration, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with limited access to HBV DNA assays. In such settings, serum ALT levels may serve as a minimum requirement for monitoring disease progression. 22. Integrating routine monitoring for HCC alongside disease progression monitoring provides an opportunity for early detection of complications.
